paragraph:
Janaka said that it was now his turn to speak of his genealogy. "There lived a king by name Nimi, who was best among men and a virtuous soul. He was known for his deeds in the three worlds. Nimi begot a son by name Mithi, who constructed the city of Mithila. He is the first Janaka, and his son was Udavasa. From him on, were Nandivardhana, Devaratha, Bhrihaddhrata, Mahavira, Sudhruti, Dhrishtaku, Hyrasva, Maru, Pratindhaka, Kiritiratha, Devamidha, Vibudha, MahIndra, Maharoma, Swarnaroma and Hrasvaroma.
Hrasvaroma begot two sons, of whom I am the first -born. Kushdhwaja is my brother. The king, my father, bequeathing the kingdom to me retired to the forest, passing on the responsibility of Kushadhwaja to me. My father is no more and I still continue my affectionate protection of my brother and rule my kingdom righteously.
Sometime ago, the king of Sankasya, Sundhava, sent a message that the sacred bow of Siva and my daughter Sita be given to him. My rejection brought about a great conflict and in the encounter between us, Sudhanva perished and I crowned Kushadhwaja, king of Sankasya. On Rama I gladly bestow Sita, my daughter who is like one, born of the gods. Urmila my other daughter I bestow on Lakshmana. The marriages will take place three days from now, under the Uttaraphalguni star".
Chapter/Canto/Verse_Reference: Bala Kanda, Sarga 71 (Janaka Narrates His Genealogy and Proposes Marriages)
Situation/Problem_Faced: Janaka reciprocates by narrating his own illustrious lineage, the Janaka dynasty, emphasizing their virtuous nature and his personal history, including his affectionate protection of his brother Kushadhwaja. He then reveals a past conflict with King Sudhanva over Siva's bow and Sita, which resulted in Sudhanva's death and Kushadhwaja's enthronement. Finally, he formally proposes the marriages of Sita to Rama and Urmila to Lakshmana, setting a date.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage highlights the importance of lineage and righteous rule in the Janaka dynasty, mirroring the Ikshvaku lineage. It establishes Janaka as a valiant and responsible ruler who protected his kingdom and family. The past conflict over the bow underscores its significance and Janaka's unwavering commitment to his vow regarding Sita. Most importantly, it formally solemnizes the marriage proposals, setting the stage for the auspicious event, and revealing that Lakshmana too receives a bride.
Outcome/Resolution: Janaka narrates his royal genealogy, starting from King Nimi. He details his personal history, including his father entrusting Kushadhwaja to his care and his righteous rule. He recounts a past conflict where he defended his kingdom and Sita from King Sudhanva, resulting in Sudhanva's defeat and Kushadhwaja's coronation. Janaka then formally proposes the marriages of Sita to Rama and Urmila to Lakshmana, scheduling them for three days hence under the Uttaraphalguni star.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Kula Dharma (Family Duty - Janaka's protection of Kushadhwaja)
Dharma (Righteousness - Janaka's rule and defense of his vow)
Sankalpa (Vow/Intention - Janaka's pledge regarding the bow)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Janaka's recitation of his 'Gotra' (lineage) establishes the spiritual purity and 'Dharma' (righteousness) of his dynasty, mirroring that of the Ikshvakus. His 'Kula Dharma' (family duty) in protecting Kushadhwaja and his steadfastness in upholding his 'Sankalpa' (vow) regarding Siva's bow, even leading to conflict, reinforces his virtuous character. The formal proposal of marriages for both Sita and Urmila, with a specific astrological alignment, emphasizes the sacred and preordained nature of these unions.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Janaka's narrative of his lineage and personal history reinforces his self-esteem** and the pride he takes in his family's virtues and his righteous rule. His affectionate protection of his brother highlights strong, positive family relationships. The recounting of the past conflict with Sudhanva, where he defended his honor and pledge, shows his resolve and capability to act decisively under pressure. The formal proposal for both Sita and Urmila to Rama and Lakshmana, respectively, brings a sense of joyful resolution and fulfillment** to his long-held desires for his daughters.
